articles.title: The Prosecution That Defined An Era — And A Genre
articles.content:
Ed. Note: Welcome to our daily feature Trivia Question of the Day!

Over eight years as a Los Angeles deputy district attorney, Vincent Bugliosi won 105 of his 106 felony jury trials, including all 21 of his murder cases. But one prosecution made him famous, a case against a cult leader who wasn’t even present at the killings he’d ordered. What is the book Bugliosi wrote about it went on to become the best-selling true-crime title in publishing history?

Hint: The case is often cited as the symbolic end of the 1960s, and the book’s two-word title has since become shorthand for chaos itself.

See the answer on the next page.

The post The Prosecution That Defined An Era — And A Genre appeared first on Above the Law.

articles.title: Content Refresh Strategy: How To Update Old Posts For New Wins
articles.content:
One of the most cost-effective techniques for ensuring your website stays relevant in search results and AI answers is to “refresh” existing content by updating posts that are more than a few months old. Because updating “old” blog posts typically takes less time and effort than starting from scratch, even with a familiar topic, in many cases these updates can yield results similar to posting a new blog entry at a fraction of the cost.
Content Refresh: Giving Your Blog Post A Makeover
If you are trying to “DIY” all of your blog content while managing your law practice, then both resources (time and attentional effort) are obviously at a premium. If you are managing your blog through the services of a freelance writer or a digital marketing agency, then the reduced expenditure of research time and content creation ingenuity on their end may lead to a monetary savings on yours (which still means a competitive ROI compared to all-new content creation that aligns with your digital marketing strategy). If you do not already have a content update fee and strategy written into your retainer agreement with them, consider this your cue to open negotiations for an option to make these blog updates a regular part of your arrangement!
Seasonal ‘Wardrobe’ Refresh: Choosing Blog Posts Ready For An Update
Not that you need to be a legal fashionista to take advantage of an update strategy to refresh your blog, but those seasonal “wardrobe refresh” articles you may have seen on the fronts of magazines in the checkout line at your local grocery store offer a surprisingly useful model for updating your law firm blog posts, not so much in the execution (please do not recommend flattering spring floral or instruct your clients in the most fashion-forward colors to rock this fall unless you have a very specific practice niche) as in the logic that goes into determining which pieces could do with a facelift and which ones need to continue doing exactly what they are doing.
Separating Staples From Seasonal Pieces
At base, the core principle in both cases is this: There are always going to be a few “classic” items that reliably deliver the desired results: day in and day out, not just season after season but year after year. Then there are some seasonally specific pieces that you will not necessarily want to “toss” in your next “closet cleanout” but may prefer to give an up-to-the-moment look, with new accessories or tailoring, when it is time to pull them out each year.
The “core” pieces are your evergreen articles (ideally these should be organized into content hubs or pillars). As with a wardrobe, on a blog in most cases you will want to leave these more or less alone; one of my writers who has a particularly folksy style of delivery in content development sessions likes to call this the “If it ain’t broke, don’t fix it” approach to managing evergreen content, and like so many pithy colloquialisms, this one expresses a genuine insight. On the other side of things, you are always going to have a few pieces that still “fit” and look seasonally appropriate for the time of year, but may be getting a bit “dated”; these are the ones that are ripe for a thorough overhaul.
What To Look For: Content Refresh Audit
The easiest and in most cases the most efficient way to go about selecting blog posts to update is to perform (or have your digital marketing agency perform) a quarterly or semi-annual content audit. I recommend quarterly if your practice provides services primarily to the general public (e.g., personal injury or family law) and has intense local competition; when the local competition for a blog’s target keyword(s) is less intense, and in practice areas where search volume for the high-intent keywords sees relatively little fluctuation, you may get a higher ROI by going with a semi-annual update schedule that gives each page, and each change, time to yield measurable results.
SEO is cumulative, so you will not want to make major changes to all of your content at the same time; instead, pick a few key pieces at the start of each audit that are up-to-date as far as their legal accuracy and that have consistently performed well since the most recent update, and make sure you leave these posts unchanged for stability as you proceed to flag and refresh other material.
Legal Accuracy
In your audit, check (or have your digital marketing agency check) the following:
• Do all outgoing and internal links work?
• Have any laws pertinent to the topics covered seen revisions since the most recent update?
•Have any filing guidelines or rules of procedure been updated in a way that alters timelines, standard court fees, or other requirements mentioned in the text?
• Has case law since the previous update affected the prevailing interpretation of any laws relevant to the topic?
Even if none of the above will directly impact the accuracy of your content, it may be worth a look to see whether there are opportunities to add detail and expand on the already-accurate information in the post as written.
Performance Metrics
Also check these performance metrics:
• Search volume and ranking difficulty for each targeted keyword (check this against these values as of the original content scheduling date)
• Page traffic, particularly visits and bounce rates
• The queries from which each post is receiving traffic (focus on the top five listed for each page in Google Search Console and compare to the top five listed at last update)
As you (or your marketing team) review the information, one thing to keep an eye on is the relationship between the pages receiving the highest inbound traffic volume and the lowest bounce rates, and the queries in which they are being found. As you review, bear in mind that highest traffic volume and lowest bounce rates do not always go hand-in-hand, so you may need to match each against the relevant queries separately to develop a nuanced picture of current blog post performance (and the direction in which it is trending).
‘Closet’ Triage: The Logic Behind Update Choices
Obviously, you should always update or remove a blog post that is no longer legally accurate. Two other criteria that should automatically prompt you to expand or refresh the existing post content, paragraph by paragraph, are:
• The entry is more than six months old.
• The keywords targeted in the blog as originally posted are no longer seeing consistent search volume.
If either of these applies, it weighs in favor of an update; if both apply, the blog post almost certainly needs a “makeover.”
Some less-definitive conditions that should nudge you to consider a refresh and how it might serve your larger SEO strategy include:
• Legal information has not changed, but the post is more than six months old.
• Other pages on your website have undergone substantial updates since publication (you may have new chances to integrate internal links!)
• Your practice has shifted its emphasis to target a specific subset of case types more aggressively (an update can give you the chance to refine the alignment of your blog post with your current trajectory).
• Search trends are moving away from your original target keywords, but the topics behind those keywords remain relevant (update the blog post to integrate new keywords).
Generally speaking, you should err on the side of updating when in doubt. How extensive those updates may need to be is another question.
Rinse And Repeat
Remember, a content refresh is something you should make a regularly scheduled part of your digital maintenance. Make it a habit and be sure to check in with your SEO team so that they are aware of any recent law firm victories or other significant achievements that demonstrate the topical expertise of one or more of your attorneys, so that appropriate links can be added at the same time your coverage of the topic is updated. Consider looking for a digital marketing agency that offers routine check-ins on a predictable schedule, so that you do not have to remember to schedule a separate discussion to cover content refresh every few months. As always, stay attuned to your local audience and clientele, and be prepared to adjust the tone and style of your blog posts as well as the “bones” of their content as needed in order to connect with the potential clients you most want to reach.
A consistent content refresh strategy helps your law firm get more value from the work you have already invested in creating. By regularly auditing existing posts, updating legal information, refining keyword targeting, and strengthening internal linking, you can improve search visibility without constantly starting from scratch. Whether you manage updates internally or work with a trusted law firm marketing agency, making content refreshes a routine part of your SEO strategy can help your website remain accurate, competitive, and relevant to both search engines and potential clients. Over time, these incremental improvements can compound into significant gains in traffic, authority, and client acquisition.
Annette Choti, Esq., has over two decades of legal experience and is the Founder & CEO of Law Quill, a concierge legal marketing agency for law firms. Annette authored the bestselling book Click Magnet: The Ultimate Guide To Digital Marketing For Law Firms, hosts the popular Legal Marketing Lounge podcast, and founded Click Magnet Academy where she teaches professionals to leverage the powerful LinkedIn platform. As a sought after speaker for Bar Associations, Legal Associations, and Marketing Conferences, Annette provides legal marketing insight along with an entertaining twist. Annette used to do theatre and professional comedy, which is not so different from the legal field if we are all being honest. Annette can be found on LinkedIn or directly through email at Annette@LawQuill.com

articles.title: The Money Mistakes High-Earning Lawyers Don’t See Coming
articles.content:
In a recent conversation with Niraj Chhabra, managing director of SideBar Advisors, I explored a problem that surprises a lot of successful attorneys: earning a high income is not the same thing as building real wealth.
What Niraj brought to the conversation was nearly two decades of experience advising lawyers on their finances, and a clear-eyed view of where even high earners quietly lose ground.
The Biggest Culprit Hiding in Plain Sight
What’s the most common financial mistake lawyers make? Here, Niraj shares the biggest culprit, which holds true at every stage of a lawyer’s career.
Why Retirement Is a Dimmer
One of the most common assumptions about retirement savings is that deferring taxes always pays off, because income, and the tax bracket that comes with it, will drop once the working years end. Niraj explained why that assumption often breaks down for lawyers.
Earning More Doesn’t Mean Saving More
Steve raised an observation from years of coaching attorneys: plenty of lawyers earn $300,000, $400,000, or $500,000 or more a year, and they work incredibly hard for it. But a strong income doesn’t automatically mean they’re saving, or investing wisely.
A Financial Plan That Grows With Your Career
The through line across this episode is that a lawyer’s financial plan can’t be set once and forgotten. Income rises, tax brackets shift, families grow, and retirement looks nothing like the clean break most people imagine.
“In other occupations, it’s an on-off switch. One day you’re in the office, one day you’re not,” Niraj says. “Attorneys nowadays, it’s more like a dimmer.”
Steve Fretzin is a five-time bestselling author, host of the BE THAT LAWYER and Future Rainmakers podcasts, and a business development coach who works exclusively with attorneys. For more than 18 years, he has helped lawyers build strong books of business without selling, pitching, or chasing, using his proven Sales-Free Selling™ approach. His clients consistently become top rainmakers and credit his coaching and systems for driving meaningful, measurable growth. Steve can be reached directly at steve@fretzin.com, or through his website at bethatlawyer.com. Connect with him on LinkedIn at https://www.linkedin.com/in/stevefretzin. His ALL NEW BE THAT LAWYER Community is changing how lawyers develop the skills never taught in law school. Learn more at bethatlawyer.com/community.
